**kernel: Offsetting, shelling, thickening** (offsetshell):
- [partial] Closed hollow shell (uniform wall, no openings) of a solid — app `ShellCommand` still hollows via mesh offset + mesh boolean. Kernel `ShellClosedSphere`/`ShellClosedTorus` (boolean.h:415-451) give an exact B-rep shell, but only for a full sphere or torus; `OffsetSolid(-t)` plus a boolean still gives a general hollow at B-rep level only via two separate calls. **New this pass:** `Mesh::Shell(thickness)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/mesh.h; src/mesh.cpp) closes the equivalent gap at mesh level directly, in one call rather than composing `Offset`+boolean by hand: it hollows an already-closed mesh into two disjoint closed layers — the original, entirely unchanged, as the outer wall, plus a flipped `Offset(-thickness)` copy as the inner wall — with no wall faces needed, since a closed mesh has no naked edge to stitch one to. Refuses a non-positive thickness, an open (not `IsClosedManifold()`) input (that case is `Thicken()`'s, not this method's), and a thickness large enough to fold the inward offset through itself or invert it past the opposite wall (checked via `FindSelfIntersections()` plus an independent enclosed-volume-ordering guard: the inner copy's own volume must land strictly between 0 and the outer's, not just be self-intersection-free — a shape thin/curved enough can silently turn inside-out without any single pair of triangles ever crossing). Still partial: mesh-level, not B-rep; no openings (see the next bullet); wall thickness is uniform, not per-face. **New this pass:** `ShellClosedSphere`/`ShellClosedTorus` (boolean.cpp) now reject a non-finite `outer_radius`/`major_radius`/`outer_minor_radius`/`thickness` — a real, previously-unguarded gap: each of these four parameters was checked only via a bare `> 0.0`/`< outer_radius`-style comparison, which is false for NaN (so NaN already threw, by accident) but TRUE for `+infinity` compared against `> 0.0`, so an infinite radius or thickness that happened to still satisfy the relative orderings (e.g. `major_radius = +inf`, a large-but-finite `outer_minor_radius < major_radius`) sailed through uncaught into `Brep::Sphere`/`ON_Torus` with an infinite dimension. Verified directly: `TestShellClosedSphereMatchesExactShellVolume` and `TestShellClosedTorusMatchesExactShellVolumeAndRejectsSpindle` (tests/test_basic.cpp) now also confirm both throw `std::invalid_argument` for a `+infinity` radius/thickness argument (and, for the sphere, a NaN `outer_radius` too, checked directly rather than assumed from the pre-existing bare comparison).
- [partial] Shell with removed/open faces (cup/case), including multi-face openings — kernel `ShellConvexPlanar` (boolean.h:340-387) is exact but convex planar solids only, and mutually-adjacent removed faces are refused. App `ShellCommand` face removal works on a mesh for simple box-like solids only. **New this pass:** `Mesh::Shell(thickness, removed_face_indices)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/mesh.h; src/mesh.cpp) is a genuine KERNEL-level mesh cup/case shell, and — unlike `ShellConvexPlanar` — not limited to convex planar solids: it removes the named faces from both the outer layer and the inward-offset inner layer, then stitches a new ring of side-wall quads around each resulting opening's own boundary, reusing `Thicken()`'s own established "one quad per naked edge, `vi = {a, b, b+n, a+n}`" construction rather than inventing a second one — the result is still a genuine closed, orientation-consistent 2-manifold (`IsClosedManifold()` holds; the cavity is exposed only through the opening's own sealed rim, not through bare naked edges). Mutually adjacent removed faces (an opening spanning several faces) are NOT refused the way `ShellConvexPlanar`'s own convex-planar assembly must refuse them — there is no equivalent topological hazard at the mesh level, verified directly (`TestMeshShellWithRemovedFaceProducesClosedManifoldCupWithStitchedWall`, tests/test_basic.cpp) on both a single removed face and two adjacent removed faces at once. Still partial: mesh-level only, not wired to any `dino8-app` command (the app's own `ShellCommand` still uses its separate, box-like-only mesh path). **New this pass:** the "not specially detected" bowtie gap just above is closed — a new file-local `ThrowIfOpeningBoundaryIsBowtie()` helper (src/mesh.cpp) refuses a removed-face set whose own post-removal naked-edge rim visits any vertex more than twice (two separate openings pinched together at a shared vertex with no shared edge between the removed faces), which neither removed-face `Shell()` overload's side-wall stitching loop can represent unambiguously (there is no way to tell, from the naked edges alone, which two of a degree-4 vertex's edges belong to which opening's own local corner). Verified on a hand-built octahedron (`MakeOctahedronMesh`, tests/test_basic.cpp) where two faces sharing exactly one vertex and no edge are removed together: `TestMeshShellRemovedFacesRefusesBowtieOpeningBoundary` confirms the refusal fires for that pair on BOTH removed-face overloads (uniform and per-face thickness), while a single removed face and two mutually EDGE-adjacent removed faces (an ordinary larger opening, not a bowtie) both still succeed — the guard is specifically about a shared vertex with no shared edge, not about "more than one removed face" in general. **New this pass:** every removed-face `Shell()` test fixture up to now leaves a remainder that stays a SINGLE connected patch — the same scope the app's own `IsSimpleManifoldWithBoundary` guard (cmd_surface.cpp) deliberately restricts itself to — so whether the kernel method itself tolerates a removal that DISCONNECTS the remainder into several separate pieces was untested, not merely unsupported. Nothing in the implementation actually assumes single-piece connectivity: its side-wall stitching loop pairs each naked edge with its own inner-offset counterpart one at a time, with no reference to which connected component it belongs to. Verified directly, not just argued: on `MakeSymmetricCubeMesh`'s own box (whose bottom and top faces share NOT ONE vertex by construction), removing all 4 side faces leaves two entirely disconnected flat squares — `TestMeshShellRemovedFacesHandlesDisconnectedRemainder` (tests/test_basic.cpp) confirms the result is still a genuine closed 2-manifold with no leftover naked edge, that both kept faces' own outer/inner vertices exactly match an independently-computed `Offset(-thickness)` on the full box, and that its enclosed volume lands strictly between 0 and the fully-closed 6-face `Shell(thickness)`'s own — real evidence this kernel method is already MORE general than the app-level guard modeled on `ShellConvexPlanar`'s own convex-planar restriction, not merely undocumented behavior. **New this pass:** the bowtie-boundary helper above is renamed `ThrowIfNakedBoundaryIsBowtie()` (from `ThrowIfOpeningBoundaryIsBowtie()`) and given a `method_name`/`boundary_description` pair so its exception text reads correctly from a caller other than an opening — see the "Thicken sheet" bullet below for why: `Mesh::Thicken()` shares this exact same degree-4-naked-vertex hazard on its own boundary and now runs the identical check.
- [partial] Per-face (multi-thickness) shell — kernel `ShellConvexPlanar` per-face overload exists (convex planar solids only). App `OffsetMeshPerFace` remains mesh-level. **New this pass:** `Mesh::Shell(const std::vector<double>& face_thickness)` (mesh.h/mesh.cpp) is the mesh-level counterpart, generalizing the uniform-thickness `Shell(double)` overload (and building on this same session's `Shell(thickness, removed_face_indices)` opening support above) to any closed 2-manifold, not just a convex planar solid. Since a mesh vertex — unlike a Brep's independently-clippable per-face planes — has no way to carry two different thicknesses on either side of it, a vertex's own offset distance is the AREA-WEIGHTED average of its incident faces' named thicknesses, the same weighting scheme `ComputeVertexNormals()` already uses for direction rather than an unweighted per-face average, an honest reconciliation rather than an approximation error. Verified two ways: a uniform `face_thickness` vector (every entry equal) reproduces `Shell(t)`'s own result up to ordinary floating-point roundoff, and on `MakeSymmetricCubeMesh`'s own equal-area square faces (where area-weighting provably degenerates to a plain average, confirmed by hand-tracing each corner's own triangle-split weights), two named corners' own actual displacement magnitudes match an independently hand-derived plain average of their 3 incident faces' thicknesses (`TestMeshShellPerFaceThicknessMatchesUniformOverloadAndHandDerivedAverages`, tests/test_basic.cpp), plus every refusal case (`TestMeshShellPerFaceThicknessRefusesInvalidInput`). Still partial: mesh-level only, no app wiring, and — unlike `ShellConvexPlanar`'s own per-face overload — a shared vertex's thickness is always a blend rather than a sharp per-face boundary, since a mesh has no analogue of a Brep's independently-clipped planes. **New this pass:** the two most recent generalizations combine — `Mesh::Shell(const std::vector<double>& face_thickness, const std::vector<int>& removed_face_indices)` (mesh.h/mesh.cpp) takes a per-face thickness vector AND an opening's removed-face list in one call, closing the "still separate" gap between this bullet and the "Shell with removed/open faces" bullet above. Construction reuses both parents' own machinery rather than inventing a third: the area-weighted per-vertex reconciliation (now factored into a shared `AreaWeightedVertexThickness()` helper used by both per-face overloads) for the offset distance, and the post-removal outer layer plus opening-boundary side-wall stitching (including the new bowtie guard above) for the opening. A removed face's own named thickness still blends into any boundary vertex it shares with a kept neighbour — the same "no special-casing removed faces" choice the uniform-thickness removed-face overload already makes for its own feasibility guard. Verified two ways, mirroring the standard each parent already holds itself to: a uniform `face_thickness` vector reproduces `Shell(thickness, removed_face_indices)`'s own result exactly (`TestMeshShellFaceThicknessWithRemovedFaceMatchesUniformOverloadAndStitchesWall`), and the same structural counts (vertex/face count, closed manifold, positive volume) the uniform-thickness removed-face overload's own test checks hold here too with a genuinely varying per-face thickness, plus the full refusal surface (`TestMeshShellFaceThicknessWithRemovedFacesRefusesInvalidInput`) and the shared bowtie-boundary refusal (`TestMeshShellRemovedFacesRefusesBowtieOpeningBoundary`). **New this pass:** both `Mesh::Shell` per-face overloads' own `face_thickness` validation now rejects a non-finite entry, not just a non-positive one — a real, previously-unguarded gap distinct from the uniform-thickness overloads' own (they call `Offset()`, which already isfinite-checks its `distance`): these two overloads instead move each vertex directly via `AreaWeightedVertexThickness()` and raw per-vertex arithmetic, with no `Offset()` call in between, so a NaN entry already happened to throw via the pre-existing `!(t > 0.0)` check but a `+infinity` entry did not (`+inf > 0.0` is true) and reached that arithmetic uncaught. Verified directly: `TestMeshShellPerFaceThicknessRefusesInvalidInput` and `TestMeshShellFaceThicknessWithRemovedFacesRefusesInvalidInput` now also confirm both overloads throw `std::invalid_argument` for a `+infinity` entry (and, for completeness, an explicit NaN case alongside it). The Brep-level sibling `ShellConvexPlanar`'s own per-face `wall_thickness` overload (boolean.cpp) had the identical gap and gets the identical fix, verified by `TestShellConvexPlanarPerFaceWallThicknessArgumentChecks` (a kept face's own `+infinity` or NaN wall_thickness entry now throws; a removed face's own entry is still never read, unchanged).

Verified (`tests/test_basic.cpp`): exact on a flat plane at every sampled point's own linearly-interpolated distance (not just at the control points the construction is built from); on a genuinely curved (bulged) freeform surface, a uniform (equal-ends) call reproduces `OffsetApproximate()`'s own result bit-for-bit; the fold guard refuses when EITHER end's own locally-interpolated distance — not just a single global one — would fold a radius-5 sphere through its own center, checked in both directions (unsafe-at-U-max-safe-at-U-min and vice versa); and the full non-finite/zero-distance argument-check surface (`OffsetVariable(NaN, ...)`, `OffsetVariable(..., +infinity)`, `OffsetVariable(0,0)` reproducing the input exactly). **Upgraded to present this pass:** `VariableOffsetSrfCommand` (cmd_srfedit.cpp) now calls this kernel method directly instead of its own inline per-CV loop, closing the app-wiring half of the gap too — verified end-to-end through the real command (`dino8-app/tests/srfedit_script.txt`'s own `VariableOffsetSrf Distance1=1 Distance2=3` fixture, re-run clean after the switch) and a non-finite-result path now surfaces as a real `ctx.Warn()` refusal instead of the silent fold the old hand-rolled version could produce.

A corner on the "cross" side of its turn (e.g. a reflex vertex under an otherwise-outward offset) is left at the exact Sharp miter-line intersection either way, since there's no gap to round there — rounding it would cut into the shape instead. A bonus of the construction: unlike `Sharp`, a `Round` fill corner never needs the miter point at all, so a turn close to a full 180 degrees (where `Sharp` refuses outright — no finite miter exists) now succeeds with a near-semicircular arc instead. Verified (`tests/test_basic.cpp`): on the same open 4-vertex polyline the existing Sharp miter tests already use, both interior (90-degree, fill) corners pass through their own independently-computed tangent points AND their own independently-computed 45-degree bisector point at exactly radius 1.0 from the vertex, while NOT passing through Sharp's own (farther, `sqrt(2)`) corner (`TestCurveOffsetInPlaneRoundStyleFilletsConvexCorners`); on the existing reflex-vertex (concave) L-tromino fixture, the one reflex corner stays at exactly Sharp's own miter point while its two convex neighbors are genuinely rounded away from theirs (`TestCurveOffsetInPlaneRoundStyleLeavesConcaveCornerAsExactMiter`); and a closed square's own Round offset closes its wraparound seam exactly and its total `Length()` matches the independent closed-form perimeter of a rounded square (4 full-length sides, unlike a chamfer, plus one full circle of radius `distance` from the four quarter-circle corners), not Sharp's own longer mitered perimeter (`TestCurveOffsetInPlaneRoundStyleClosedSquareMatchesClosedFormPerimeter`). Verified on the same three fixtures Round's own tests already establish: the open 4-vertex polyline's two fill corners pass through `T0`/`T1` and the chord's own independently-computed midpoint (radius `1/sqrt(2)` from the vertex) while missing both Sharp's farther corner and Round's farther bisector point (`TestCurveOffsetInPlaneChamferStyleCutsConvexCorners`); the L-tromino's one reflex corner stays at Sharp's own miter point while its convex neighbors are genuinely cut (`TestCurveOffsetInPlaneChamferStyleLeavesConcaveCornerAsExactMiter`); and a closed square's own Chamfer offset closes its seam exactly with total length matching the closed-form chamfered-square perimeter (4 full sides plus four `distance*sqrt(2)` chords), strictly shorter than Round's own arc-cornered perimeter at the same distance (`TestCurveOffsetInPlaneChamferStyleClosedSquareMatchesClosedFormPerimeter`). Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite re-run clean: 0 failures. This bullet's own category-row present/partial/missing counts are unchanged (this corner is still `[partial]`, just more capable), so no re-score arithmetic follows from this pass.

- [present] Curve offset on surface (in-surface, geodesic-style) — **upgraded from partial.** `NurbsCurve::OffsetInSurface(surface, distance, out, sample_count)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/curve.h; src/surface_intersect.cpp) closes the "App-only" gap this bullet used to name: the identical sample + tangent-cross-normal + re-project technique `dino8-app`'s own `OffsetCrvOnSrfCommand` (cmd_curves2.cpp) previously implemented entirely by hand, now a real kernel entry point built on `NurbsSurface::ClosestPointParameter()`/`NormalAt()`/`PointAt()` and the existing `ChordParams()`/`InterpolateCubic()` free functions `OffsetOnSurfaceNormal()` already uses, not a third separate helper set. Explicitly NOT the same operation as the sibling `OffsetOnSurfaceNormal()` (which moves OFF the surface along its normal, radius/height unchanged): this moves SIDEWAYS, along `TangentAt(t) x surface_normal`, then re-projects the moved sample back onto the surface via a second `ClosestPointParameter()` + `PointAt()` round trip — the step that actually keeps the result ON the surface, since a straight sideways step off a curved surface does not generally land back on it on its own. Calling this "geodesic-style" rather than a true geodesic offset is deliberate honesty inherited unchanged from the app technique it replaces: it moves a fixed extrinsic distance along a tangent-plane direction and snaps back, not an intrinsically-measured geodesic-normal offset — accurate wherever the surface's curvature is mild relative to `distance`, the same approximation Rhino's own OffsetCrvOnSrf already carries. An open curve of degree 1 is rebuilt as an exact degree-1 polyline through the offset samples; any other curve (higher degree, or closed) is refit as a global chord-length cubic interpolant, closed-aware — the same convention `OffsetOnSurfaceNormal()` already uses. Verified (`tests/test_basic.cpp`): on a flat plane, the result matches `OffsetInPlane`'s own explicit-plane overload point-for-point everywhere sampled — an independent cross-check, since both methods reduce to the identical `TangentAt(t) x normal` formula there and re-projecting onto a flat plane changes nothing; an open degree-1 polyline's two endpoints land exactly at `original + distance*(tangent x normal)`, computed independently of this method's own construction; a closed circle in the plane stays an exact concentric circle (every sampled point at the SAME radius from the center, not just one point checked in isolation); and, on a genuinely curved (bulged) freeform surface, this method's own output lands ON the surface (near-zero closest-surface-point distance) while `OffsetOnSurfaceNormal()`'s output on the identical curve/surface/distance lands OFF it by roughly the offset distance — direct proof the two methods solve different problems, not merely named differently. The full non-finite-distance/too-few-samples argument-check surface is covered too. **Upgraded to present this pass:** `OffsetCrvOnSrfCommand` (cmd_curves2.cpp) now calls this kernel method directly instead of its own inline per-sample tangent/normal/reproject loop, closing the app-wiring half of the gap too.
- [present] Curve offset normal to surface (OffsetNormal) — **upgraded from partial.** `NurbsCurve::OffsetOnSurfaceNormal(surface, distance, out, sample_count)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/curve.h; src/surface_intersect.cpp) closes the "App-only" gap this bullet used to name: the identical sample + closest-surface-point + normal-offset + refit technique `dino8-app`'s own `OffsetNormal` command (cmd_remaining.cpp) previously implemented entirely by hand, now a real kernel entry point built on the kernel's own `NurbsSurface::ClosestPointParameter()`/`NormalAt()` and the existing `InterpolateCubic()`/`ChordParams()` free functions (surface_intersect.h) rather than the app's own separate `SampleCurve`/`InterpolateCubic`/`PolylineCurve` helpers. An open curve of degree 1 is rebuilt as an exact degree-1 polyline through the offset samples (not smoothed into a cubic); any other curve (higher degree, or closed) is refit as a global chord-length cubic interpolant, closed-aware. This is explicitly NOT the separate, harder "Curve offset on surface" item (an in-surface, geodesic-style offset) — this moves along the surface's normal, off the surface entirely, exactly as the app technique it replaces always did. Verified (`tests/test_basic.cpp`): on a flat-plane fixture (where the exact answer is just the input curve translated by the surface's own constant normal, an independent closed-form ground truth, not a re-run of this method's own construction), both a degree-3 open curve and a closed circle stay close to their own exact translated curve all the way around (compared via `NurbsCurve::ClosestPoint()` since the refit's chord-length parameterization doesn't correspond to the original curve's own parameter); an open degree-1 polyline input stays an exact polyline, with its two endpoints landing exactly on point+distance*normal; and the full non-finite-distance/too-few-samples argument-check surface. **Upgraded to present this pass:** the app's `OffsetNormal` command (cmd_remaining.cpp) now calls this kernel method directly instead of its own inline sample/offset/refit loop, closing the app-wiring half of the gap too — verified end-to-end through the real command (a plane plus a line segment lying on it, offset by a kernel-backed `OffsetNormal` call producing a genuine new curve with no crash, since this exact command path had no prior smoke-test coverage to regress).
- [partial] Curve offset in an arbitrary plane / 3D (non-planar) curve offset — kernel `OffsetInPlane` works in the curve's own fitted plane but returns Failed for non-planar curves. The app Offset command uses only the active CPlane normal. No 3D offset. **New this pass:** `NurbsCurve::OffsetInPlane(const ON_Plane&, distance, out, tolerance)` (curve.h/curve.cpp) is a new overload that takes the caller's own plane instead of auto-fitting one, closing both gaps this bullet names at once — it no longer requires this curve to be planar at all (the direction `TangentAt(t) x plane.zaxis` is well-defined for a genuinely non-planar 3D curve too, sampled and tolerance-refit the same way the existing overload's general case already works), and it lets the caller pick ANY plane, not only this curve's own fitted one (an exact-line offset generalizes for free to any plane whose normal isn't parallel to the line; both `OffsetInPlane` overloads now share that line case and the general sampled-refit case via two new private helpers, `OffsetLineAlongNormal`/`OffsetGeneralAlongNormal`, rather than duplicating the loop). Still partial: an arc/circle offset by a plane other than its own is not special-cased to stay exactly circular (falls to the same approximate sampled path as any other curve - offsetting a circle along a foreign normal generally isn't a circle at all, so this is honest, not a shortcut), and the app's `Offset` command still doesn't call either overload with anything but the active CPlane.

Still partial: an area-weighted vertex-normal push does not preserve wall thickness at creases, and folds are not repaired. **New this pass:** `Mesh::Offset`/`Mesh::OffsetDirectional` (mesh.h/mesh.cpp) now reject a non-finite (NaN or +/-infinity) `distance` up front — a real, previously-unguarded silent-corruption gap, not a hypothetical one: before this pass, `distance == 0.0` was the only check either method made (`OffsetDirectional`'s own zero-vector-direction check is unrelated and stays as-is), so a NaN or infinite `distance` sailed straight through and got baked into every vertex — and since a NaN/Inf coordinate makes most downstream numeric comparisons resolve to false rather than true, a fold/self-intersection guard built on top of either method (`Shell()`'s and `Thicken()`'s own `FindSelfIntersections()` calls) could not be relied on to catch the corruption either, only its own accidental side effects. Still partial for the reasons already named above — this closes an input-validation gap, not the disclosed crease/fold limitation.
- [partial] SubD offset / thicken — app `OffsetNet` (cmd_subd.cpp:595) offsets the control net (not the limit surface); Solid adds a flipped copy plus side quads. **New this pass:** the "No kernel SubD offset" half of this gap is closed — `SubD::Offset(distance)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/subd.h; src/subd.cpp) moves every control-net vertex along its own EXACT Catmull-Clark limit-surface normal (`LimitPoints()`'s own `limit_normal`), a genuine improvement in direction over the app's existing control-net-normal technique: the control net's own facets generally aren't tangent to the limit surface the way the limit normal is by definition, so the two only coincide exactly where a vertex's one-ring happens to already be planar. Unlike `Weld()`'s own snapshot-and-rebuild-a-fresh-`ON_SubD` technique (needed there because welding changes topology), this delegates directly to the real `ON_SubDVertex::SetControlNetPoint(point, bClearNeighborhoodCache)` primitive (verified by reading `opennurbs_subd_data.cpp`: it updates the vertex's own point and invalidates every neighboring edge's/face's cached subdivision point) since an offset never changes topology at all — every vertex/edge/face id, every edge tag and crease sharpness, stays exactly as it was, nothing to remap or re-derive. A vertex whose own limit normal is undefined (the zero vector, per `SubDLimitPoint`'s own documented convention) is left unmoved, the same fallback `Mesh::ComputeVertexNormals()`/`Mesh::Offset()` already use for a degenerate mesh-vertex normal. Still only an approximate offset, the same honest caveat every other per-vertex offset in this codebase already carries (`Mesh::Offset()`, `NurbsSurface::OffsetApproximate()`): moving each vertex independently along its own current limit normal does not reproduce the limit surface a hypothetical "offset cage" would itself subdivide to, since Catmull-Clark subdivision is not a one-vertex-at-a-time local operation. Verified (`tests/test_basic.cpp`) against the exact closed-form ground truth `TestSubDLimitPointsExactCubeAndFlatGrid` already establishes independently (every cube-cage corner's limit normal is its own exact unit outward body diagonal): `Offset(+0.3)` on a cube cage moves every corner by exactly `0.3 * diagonal`, not the cruder control-net (face-average) normal (which would only happen to agree here by this cube's own high symmetry), changes no topology, leaves the original SubD untouched, and `Offset(0.0)` is an exact identity on every vertex position; the full non-finite-distance argument-check surface (NaN, +/-infinity) is covered too. Still partial: this is a whole-cage uniform-distance offset only (no per-face/per-vertex thickness, no removed-face/opening support the way `Mesh::Shell()` has), no Solid (thicken-into-a-closed-shell) variant, and no app command calls it — `dino8-app`'s own `OffsetNet` still offsets the raw control net by hand, unchanged. **New this pass (2026-10-05):** the "no Solid variant" half of this gap is closed — `SubD::Thicken(distance, tessellation_tolerance, max_resolution)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/subd.h; src/subd.cpp) tessellates this SubD's own LIMIT SURFACE via the existing `Tessellate()` and hands the result straight to the existing `Mesh::Thicken()` — a thin, honest composition of two already-independently-tested kernel methods, not a new offset/stitching algorithm of its own, and a genuine accuracy improvement over the app's `OffsetNet` Solid option, which still thickens the raw CONTROL NET by hand rather than the smooth limit surface. A real, not hypothetical, latent bug caught and fixed before landing: `Loft()`'s own `cap` option is meant for a tube swept between profiles at the SAME station (a disk bounded by one profile closes the end); for a ribbon between a CLOSED curve and its own offset, the two sections are DIFFERENT curves, so a disk capped to just the first one would ignore the offset entirely rather than closing the annular strip between them — `RibbonFromCurve` always passes `cap=false`, verified directly (not merely argued) on a circle: the result stays a genuine 1-face, non-solid annular strip, not a wrongly-capped tube. - [partial] Exact analytic-face offset (plane->plane, cylinder->cylinder, cone->cone, sphere->sphere with shifted radius) — **corrected: the cylinder branch keeps a partial patch's own angular extent (prior pass); this pass, the cone branch keeps BOTH its angular AND axial extent too — still partial.** `NurbsSurface::OffsetAnalytic`'s cylinder case (surface.cpp) previously always called `ON_Cylinder::GetNurbForm()` and returned it as-is, silently ballooning a partial patch (e.g. a quarter-cylinder fillet face) into a closed 360-degree tube. It now measures the input patch's own true angular span geometrically (`ON_Circle::ClosestPointTo` at both U-domain ends, independent of either cylinder's radius since offset and original share the same `circle.plane`), converts that span through `ON_Circle::GetNurbFormParameterFromRadian` — required because a circle's NURBS parameter is a rational-quadratic reparametrization, not linear in angle, except at the four quadrant knots — and `Trim()`s the freshly-built full cylinder down to it, so the offset keeps the same angular extent the input had. A full/closed input cylinder (U-domain already spanning a full turn) is detected up front and left untrimmed, exactly reproducing the prior (correct) behavior for that case. Verified on a quarter-turn patch of a radius-4, height-10 cylinder offset by +1.0: every sampled point on the result still sits at exactly radius 5.0 from the axis (same exactness the full-cylinder case already had), the U-min and U-max boundary curves sit at true angle 0 and pi/2 respectively (not anywhere else on the circle), and the trimmed U-domain span is a small fraction of a full turn's own span rather than the whole circle (`TestSurfaceOffsetAnalyticCylinderPreservesQuarterPatchExtent`, tests/test_basic.cpp). **New this pass:** the cone branch had the SAME defect in both its own directions at once — `ON_Cone::GetNurbForm()` always builds a full 360-degree cone running from the literal apex (height_parameter 0) out to whatever `height` it's given, so the prior code (which just reused the ORIGINAL cone's own `height`/`radius` pair unchanged, only translating the apex) silently ballooned a partial patch angularly (same issue as the cylinder) AND axially (a fillet-style frustum band that touches neither the apex nor the base would balloon all the way down to the apex). The angular half reuses the cylinder branch's own technique verbatim (one shared reference circle works for both the old and new cone, since the new cone's plane is the old one's translated ONLY along its own zaxis, which cannot change a point's projected angle). The axial half is genuinely different from the cylinder case, and can't reuse its "leave the original bounds alone" shortcut: a cone's offset shifts axial position too (the apex itself moves along the axis), and — unlike the angular case — the v-domain boundary can BE the apex, a singular point with no well-defined normal to offset along. The fix proves (and the code comment derives) that the offset image's axial position is an exact, angle-independent, slope-1 affine function of the original axial position, measures that function's one free constant at the safely-interior domain midpoint (never a boundary), then applies it to the actual v-domain boundaries via plain axial projection (a dot product, safe even exactly at the apex) — and, since the true offset extent can now run past the original cone's own arbitrary `height` value, the pre-trim substrate cone is sized from the computed extent itself rather than reusing the original `(height, radius)` pair verbatim (which could otherwise be too short to trim down to the real range, a latent bug the fix also closes). A patch straddling the apex on both sides at once — impossible to represent as a single `ON_Cone::GetNurbForm()` nappe — is refused. Verified on a quarter-turn (angular), mid-height-band (axial, touching neither apex nor base) patch of the same radius-5, height-10 cone offset by +1.0: the angular boundaries sit at true angle 0 and pi/2 exactly as the cylinder case's own test checks, and — the axial fix's own direct proof — the output's own v-domain MIN and MAX boundary points are each bit-exact (`< 1e-6`) matches of the INPUT patch's corresponding v-domain boundary point plus `distance * NormalAt(...)` there, evaluated at the identical true angle on each surface's own domain despite their differing nonlinear NURBS parameter values, with the output's own v-span confirmed to be a small fraction of the full apex-to-base height rather than the whole cone (`TestSurfaceOffsetAnalyticConePreservesPartialPatchExtent`, tests/test_basic.cpp); the pre-existing `TestSurfaceOffsetAnalyticConePreservesHalfAngleAndShiftsApex` (a FULL, apex-touching cone) needed its own golden-section search bracket widened from a hardcoded guess to the output's own actual (now genuinely narrower, apex-excluding) domain, since that is exactly the behavior this fix intentionally introduces. **New this pass:** the sphere branch had the same defect in BOTH its own directions at once (longitude in u, latitude in v) — `ON_Sphere::GetNurbForm()` always builds the full 360-degree-by-180-degree primitive, so the prior code (which reused `ON_Sphere(center, radius)`'s own default plane unchanged) silently ballooned any partial patch (e.g. a spherical fillet/lens face) back to the whole sphere. Fixing it surfaced a real bug one level up: `ON_Sphere(center, radius)`'s own constructor always resets `plane` to the world `ON_xy_plane` (`opennurbs_sphere.cpp`'s `Create()`), discarding the input sphere's own orientation — invisible on a full sphere (isotropic, no seam to misplace) but fatal to any orientation-dependent trim. The fix does NOT simply copy the input's own fitted `plane` back, though: `ON_Surface::IsSphere()`'s own fallback fit (`opennurbs_revsurface.cpp`) samples both an equator-style isocurve and a meridian-style isocurve, each `IsArc()`-fitted into its own candidate `ON_Sphere::plane`, and returns whichever ONE happens to validate first — a sphere's rotational symmetry makes either an equally valid "some center/radius fit", but the two are genuinely different (rotated) frames, and for anything short of a full untrimmed sphere there is no way to know in advance which one `IsSphere()` handed back. So the fix derives its own frame directly from sampled points on the actual input surface instead of trusting `IsSphere()`'s own `plane` at all: a latitude circle's own plane is perpendicular to the polar axis by definition, so 3 points at the same v and 3 distinct u fractions (never the exact domain ends, so a full/closed loop's own coincident seam can't degenerate the fit) pin down that axis, and the first of the 3 (at the input's own u-domain minimum) fixes the equatorial xaxis — the same self-derived frame is then used to build `new_sphere.plane` before calling its own `GetNurbForm()`, guaranteeing the output's raw u/v convention matches what the trim math measures. A second, genuinely separate bug surfaced verifying this against a deliberately non-world-aligned sphere (world-aligned inputs can't expose either bug, by luck): the u-domain's own minimum sample sits EXACTLY on the derived xaxis by construction — the single worst point for `ClosestPointTo`'s `[0, 2pi)` wraparound, where ordinary float noise can push the measured angle to a hair below 0 (fine) or a hair above 2*pi's own wrap boundary (silently landing at ~2*pi instead of ~0, flipping a genuine short arc's own two ends to look like the long way around the circle) — fixed by re-expressing both u-domain ends within +-pi of the (always safely domain-interior) midpoint before comparing, then clamping the result back into `[0, 2pi]` before `Trim()`. Verified (`TestSurfaceOffsetAnalyticSpherePreservesPartialPatchExtent`, tests/test_basic.cpp) on a quarter-longitude, equator-to-north-pole quarter-latitude patch of a sphere whose polar axis is deliberately NOT any world axis: every sampled point on the offset patch sits at exactly the offset radius from the same center; the u-domain's two boundaries sit at true longitude 0 and pi/2 measured against the ORIGINAL (rotated) frame, not wherever a mismatched frame would place them; the v-domain's two boundaries sit at true latitude 0 (equator) and pi/2 (north pole) the same way; both domain spans are well under their own full untrimmed range; and the pre-existing self-intersection guard (an inward offset exceeding the radius) still refuses on this same partial patch. Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite re-run clean: 100% passing, 0 regressions. **New this pass:** the torus branch had the same "GetNurbForm() always builds the FULL primitive" defect in BOTH its own directions (major angle in u, minor angle in v) — `ON_Torus::GetNurbForm()` always builds the complete 360x360-degree primitive, so the prior code (which reused `torus.plane`/`major_radius` unchanged and only shifted `minor_radius`) silently ballooned any partial patch (e.g. a torus-fillet lens face) back to the whole donut. Torus turns out to be the ONLY one of the four analytic families whose `GetNurbForm()` builds via the generic `ON_RevSurface::TensorProduct` path rather than a dedicated direct construction (confirmed by reading `opennurbs_torus.cpp`/`opennurbs_revsurface.cpp`, not assumed) — and that path rescales BOTH the raw `[0, 2*pi]` rational-quadratic circle parameter the sphere/cylinder/cone branches already convert via `GetNurbFormParameterFromRadian()` into ARC-LENGTH units instead (`[0, 2*pi*major_radius]` for u, `[0, 2*pi*minor_radius]` for v) — confirmed directly against `GetNurbForm()`'s own output domain, not assumed from reading the source alone. So converting a measured true angle to this surface's own domain value needs the usual conversion PLUS one extra multiply by the relevant radius, using the OFFSET tube radius (not the original) for v, since unlike `major_radius` the tube radius genuinely changes under this offset. A second, genuinely separate discovery made verifying this: `ON_Torus::ClosestPointTo()`'s own `minor_angle` output is a real, previously-undiscovered OpenNURBS bug — its internal arithmetic subtracts a bare direction vector (`major_radius*raxis`) from the absolute query point without first subtracting `plane.origin`, silently assuming the torus is centered at the world origin; invisible on a world-centered fixture (the existing coaxial-torus test above never exposed it) and confirmed wrong by over a tenth of a radian on an off-origin one. Worked around, the same way the cylinder branch above already works around its own `circle.plane.ClosestPointTo` bug: minor angle is measured via `MinorCircleRadians(major_angle)`'s OWN `ClosestPointTo` (an entirely different, independently-verified-exact code path) instead. A defensive convention check also guards the one remaining ambiguity `IsTorus()`'s own fallback fit shares with `IsSphere()`'s (above): a surface built with u/v transposed from the ordinary (u=major, v=minor) convention is refused rather than mishandled, verified directly (does moving along u change major_angle, as expected, or minor_angle?) rather than trusted. Verified (`TestSurfaceOffsetAnalyticTorusPreservesPartialPatchExtent`, `TestSurfaceOffsetAnalyticTorusOffOriginTiltedPreservesArbitraryPatchExtent`, `TestSurfaceOffsetAnalyticTorusRefusesTransposedConvention`, tests/test_basic.cpp) on a world-aligned quarter-major/half-minor patch (every sampled point at exactly the offset tube radius; u/v boundaries at true angle 0 and pi/2 or pi via direct atan2/radius checks; both domain spans well under a full turn) and, more adversarially, an off-origin, non-axis-aligned torus trimmed to arbitrary (non-knot-aligned) major and minor sub-ranges (same tube-radius check; all 4 domain corners land exactly on this patch's own point + distance*normal, the strong check that catches a merely-plausible-looking wrong sub-range) — plus the transposed-convention refusal. Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite re-run clean: 5864 checks passing, 0 regressions (one known-intermittent, unrelated `FoldFaceConvexPlanar` flake — see this document's own prior note on it — reproduced on one run and was absent on a clean rerun of the same unchanged binary). Still partial: a patch whose angular span straddles either circle parametrization's own seam (verified via a midpoint-inside-range check, same as the other branches) is refused rather than mishandled, and it is still a single-surface operation, not a face within a B-rep. Every analytic branch this method has (plane, cylinder, cone, sphere, torus) now keeps the domain and trim.

Growth is checked against a real, convexity-independent closed form the existing convex-only Steiner-formula test above can't reuse: a Minkowski sum with a ball of radius `d` expands the axis-aligned bounding box by EXACTLY `d` on every one of the 6 sides for ANY compact solid, reflex edges included, since the solid and the ball attain their own per-axis extremes independently (`bbox_max_x(P (+) B) = bbox_max_x(P) + max_b(b.x) = bbox_max_x(P) + d`) — verified to hold exactly on this fixture, plus `IsClosedManifold()` and a strictly-larger-volume check. - [partial] OpenNURBS-native mesh offset, ON_Mesh::OffsetMesh(distance, direction) — `ON_Mesh::OffsetMesh` is still never called. **New this pass:** the fixed-direction variant this bullet's own prior text said had "no kernel counterpart" now does: `Mesh::OffsetDirectional(distance, direction)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/mesh.h; src/mesh.cpp) moves every vertex by the identical vector `distance * direction.UnitVector()`, never consulting any per-vertex normal at all — genuinely distinct from the existing `Mesh::Offset(distance)` (which moves each vertex along its OWN `ComputeVertexNormals()` direction), not a renamed duplicate: translating every point of a flat region by one shared vector keeps that region exactly planar regardless of a neighboring crease's own curvature (`Offset()` can't make that guarantee, since a crease-adjacent vertex's averaged normal differs from an isolated flat vertex's), at the honest cost of no longer keeping wall thickness uniform across a curved region (every vertex moves the same amount along `direction`, not the locally-true normal) — the same disclosed tradeoff the fixed-direction OpenNURBS variant itself has. `direction` need not be a unit vector (normalized internally); a zero vector is refused (`std::invalid_argument`), since there is no well-defined unit direction to offset along. Verified on a flat unit square (reproduces `Offset()`'s own result exactly when `direction` matches the square's normal, and confirms a non-unit `direction` still moves by exactly `distance` along its unit form, not `distance` times the vector's own magnitude) and, more adversarially, on a V-groove fixture (two non-parallel walls meeting at a shared apex edge, reused from `FindOffsetSelfIntersections`'s own test): `OffsetDirectional()` moves every vertex — apex and wall-top alike — by the exact same displacement vector, while a control `Offset()` call on the identical groove is independently confirmed to move at least one vertex by a genuinely DIFFERENT vector (the apex's own averaged normal differs from a wall-top vertex's) — proving the two methods solve different problems, not merely checking each in isolation (`TestMeshOffsetDirectionalMovesEveryVertexByTheSameFixedVector`, tests/test_basic.cpp). Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite (via `ctest`) re-run clean: 100% passing, 0 regressions (one known-intermittent, unrelated `FoldFaceConvexPlanar` flake — see this document's own prior note on it — reproduced on one run and was absent on a clean rerun of the same unchanged binary). Still partial: face topology is untouched (no fold repair or self-intersection handling — the same disclosed hazard `Offset()` already has, inherited here rather than newly introduced), `ON_Mesh::OffsetMesh` itself is still never called, and no app command calls this new kernel entry point.
- [partial] Inset (offset mesh/SubD/polysurface face edges inward toward face center) — app `InsetFaces` (cmd_subd.cpp:544) moves each corner toward the face centroid, not a true in-plane edge-parallel inset; SubD only. **New this pass:** kernel `Mesh::InsetFace(face_index, distance, depth)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/mesh.h; src/mesh.cpp) is a genuine in-plane, edge-parallel mesh inset: every edge of the named triangle or quad face moves inward parallel to its own original direction, and each new corner is the exact mitered intersection of its two adjacent moved edges — the same construction sweep.cpp's own `OffsetConvexPolyline` already uses for a curve profile, applied here to one mesh face's closed boundary ring instead. The original face is replaced by a ring of `n` new "frame" quads (one per original edge) plus one new inner face at the inset ring, every new vertex staying exactly coplanar with the original face (`depth`, if nonzero, additionally lifts only the inner ring along the face's own normal — the bevelled/pushed variant of the same tool). Verified on a flat unit-square face (distance 0.25, an exact power-of-two fraction chosen so the check survives `ON_3fPoint`'s own float vertex storage without a spurious rounding mismatch): the 4 new corners exactly match the hand-derived concentric inset square, and total mesh area is conserved exactly — a flat inset only subdivides the same planar region, it can't add or remove material (`TestMeshInsetFaceUnitSquareMatchesExactConcentricSquare`). Also verified on a non-axis-aligned 3-4-5 right triangle via an INDEPENDENT point-to-line distance check (not a re-run of this method's own miter formula): every new corner sits at exactly `distance` from both of its two adjacent original edge LINES (`TestMeshInsetFaceTriangleMatchesIndependentPerpendicularDistance`). Refusal cases covered: an out-of-range `face_index`, a non-positive `distance`, a distance reaching or exceeding the face's own inradius (folds a corner past the opposite side), a non-planar ("warped") quad, and a concave (reflex-cornered) but still simple quad (`TestMeshInsetFaceRefusesInvalidInput`); `depth`'s own inner-ring-only lift is checked separately (`TestMeshInsetFaceDepthLiftsInnerRingAlongNormal`). Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite (via `ctest`) re-run clean: 100% passing, 0 regressions. Still partial, and deliberately narrow: one triangle or quad face at a time (an `ON_Mesh` face can be no larger — no general n-gon), convex only (a reflex corner throws rather than being handled, the same scope every other convex-planar-ring construction in this category already has), no SubD or Brep-level inset, and `dino8-app`'s own `InsetFaces` still only does the centroid-drag approximation — a grep for InsetFace in dino8-app/src still finds nothing. **New this pass:** `InsetFace`'s own `distance` and `depth` parameters gain the same non-finite hardening this category's own recent passes already gave `Mesh::Offset`/`Thicken`/`Shell`. `distance`'s pre-existing `!(distance > 0.0)` check already caught NaN by accident but not `+infinity` (`+inf > 0.0` is true) — and an infinite `distance` is a genuinely worse silent-corruption case here than in those other methods: it turns each mitered corner into a difference of two points already moved to infinity in different directions, which can itself evaluate to NaN, and the very next guard this method runs (`ON_DotProduct(e, edir[i]) <= 0.0`, meant to catch a distance past the face's own inradius) is a comparison that a NaN also silently defeats — so without this pass's fix, an infinite `distance` could reach the end of the function and return a mesh with NaN/infinite vertex positions, refused by neither guard. `depth` previously had no check at all (only a bare `depth != 0.0` before adding `depth * normal` to every inset vertex, true for both NaN and infinity, with nothing downstream to catch either). Both parameters now reject non-finite input up front. Verified directly: `TestMeshInsetFaceRefusesInvalidInput` (tests/test_basic.cpp) now also confirms `std::invalid_argument` for a NaN or `+infinity` `distance`, and for a NaN or infinite `depth`. **New this pass (2026-10-06):** the "no SubD or Brep-level inset" half of this gap closes at the Brep level — `InsetPlanarFace(solid, face_index, distance, depth)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/boolean.h; src/boolean.cpp) is `Mesh::InsetFace()`'s own exact mitered-corner construction applied to `Brep::PlanarFace`'s arbitrary-length polygon `loop` instead of a triangle/quad-only `ON_MeshFace` — a genuine generalization, not a mere relocation: `Mesh::InsetFace()`'s own "one triangle or quad face at a time" restriction came entirely from `ON_MeshFace`'s own representation, not from anything about the mitered-offset algorithm itself, so this closes that restriction too, for any n-gon. A further, real scope improvement over this whole family's usual precondition: unlike `OffsetFace()`/`ShellConvexPlanar()` above, `InsetPlanarFace()` does NOT require `solid` as a whole to be convex — insetting one face only ever replaces THAT face (with `n` new frame quads plus one new inner face), never touching any other face's own plane or boundary, so whatever manifoldness the rest of `solid` already has survives automatically through `FromPlanarFaces()`'s own vertex-welding; only the NAMED face itself must be convex (the same precondition `Mesh::InsetFace()` already carries, for the identical self-intersection reason). Verified (`tests/test_basic.cpp`) on a 10x10x10 box's own top face: `distance=2.0, depth=0.0` (pure in-plane inset) gives exactly 10 faces (6 - 1 + 1 inner + 4 frame) and leaves the TOTAL enclosed volume bit-for-bit unchanged at 1000 — a flat inset adds or removes no material, a real closed-form check — while the other 5 faces keep their own loop points exactly where they started (`TestInsetPlanarFaceOnBoxTopFaceFlatMatchesUnchangedVolumeAndCorrectTopology`); `distance=1.0, depth=0.5` (the inset ring raised along the face's own outward normal) matches the independently-derivable exact pyramidal-frustum-volume closed form, `(depth/3)(A0 + A1 + sqrt(A0*A1))` between the original (area 100) and raised inset (area 64) boundaries, not merely a plausible-looking number (`TestInsetPlanarFaceOnBoxTopFaceWithDepthMatchesExactFrustumVolume`); and the full argument-check surface (out-of-range `face_index`, non-positive/non-finite `distance`, non-finite `depth`, a distance reaching or exceeding the face's own inradius) is covered (`TestInsetPlanarFaceArgumentChecks`). Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite re-run clean: all checks passing, 0 regressions. Re-reading this category's remaining bullets fresh turned up a SECOND, subtler failure mode the prior sweep's own grep pattern couldn't catch, because on its face each site already had a distance/thickness guard: a bare `!(x > 0.0)`-style check silently rejects NaN (any comparison against NaN is false, so the negation is true) but NOT `+infinity` (`+inf > 0.0` IS true, so the negation is false and the value passes) — the exact inverse blind spot from the prior pass's `== 0.0` sites, and easy to miss precisely because the existing guard reads as complete. Traced each site all the way to where the resulting NaN/Inf value is actually consumed, not just to the first guard, since several of these route through a SECOND comparison-based guard downstream (an area or self-intersection check) that a naive read might assume catches what the first one missed — several of those second guards turned out to have the identical NaN blind spot, silently waving through exactly the corrupted input the first guard let past. Eight sites across two files fixed, each verified by extending an existing regression test (no new test functions, so no discovery-order dependency to document) rather than one deep dive: (1)/(2) `Mesh::Shell(face_thickness)` and `Mesh::Shell(face_thickness, removed_face_indices)` (mesh.cpp) — unlike the uniform-thickness `Shell(thickness)` overloads (already safe: they call `Offset()`, which the prior pass hardened), these two move every vertex directly via `AreaWeightedVertexThickness()`, with no `Offset()` call in between, so a `+infinity` entry in `face_thickness` reached that arithmetic uncaught even after the prior pass landed; (3) `Mesh::InsetFace`'s `distance` (mesh.h/mesh.cpp) — the worse case in this batch, since an infinite `distance` doesn't just produce an infinite vertex, it can produce a NaN one (a mitered corner is a DIFFERENCE of two already-infinite points moved in different directions), which then silently defeats the very next guard (`ON_DotProduct(e, edir[i]) <= 0.0`, meant to catch a too-large `distance`) the same way; `InsetFace`'s own `depth` parameter had no check at all (`depth != 0.0` is true for both NaN and infinity) and gets one for the first time; (4) `ShellConvexPlanar`'s per-face `wall_thickness` overload (boolean.cpp), the Brep-level sibling of fixes (1)/(2) above, with the identical `!(t > 0.0)` blind spot; (5)/(6) `ShellClosedSphere`/`ShellClosedTorus` (boolean.cpp) — each of `outer_radius`/`major_radius`/`outer_minor_radius`/`thickness` used the same bare-comparison pattern, so e.g. an infinite `major_radius` could still satisfy `outer_minor_radius < major_radius` for a large-but-finite `outer_minor_radius` and reach `ON_Torus`/`Brep::Sphere` with an infinite dimension; (7) `OffsetFace` (boolean.cpp) — its `distance` parameter had NO validation at all before this pass (not even the accidental-NaN-rejection the other sites had), so both NaN and infinity reached `ClipConvexPolygon`/`PlanarPolygonArea` uncaught, and the resulting NaN/Inf area then silently defeated the pre-existing `area <= area_tol` degenerate-face guard too (a NaN comparison is never true); A real, found-by-testing defect surfaced only once a genuinely shared edge was tried (never exercised before, since every prior test was naked/single-trim): for whichever of a shared edge's two trims has `m_bRev3d == true` (its own 2D direction opposite the edge's 3D one — exactly one side of ANY shared edge by the ordinary convention), unconditionally committing the new trims with `bRev3d == false` spliced them into that face's own loop in the wrong relative order — same trim count, same two edges, `Check()` entirely unaware — producing a genuinely self-crossing loop that only a tessellated-area check exposed (3x the true area on that one face). Fixed by keeping each trim's own two split pieces in their natural domain order (always the loop's own walk order, `bRev3d` or not) and choosing which physical edge piece each one references, with `bRev3d` flipped to `true` only on the side that needs it. - [partial] Move/transform face (tweak face, neighbours adjust) — **corrected: gained a real kernel rigid-transform implementation, still partial.** `MoveFaceConvexPlanar(solid, face_index, xform)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/boolean.h; dino8-kernel/src/boolean.cpp) now exists: `xform` (an `ON_Xform`) is applied directly to `face_index`'s own current plane via `ON_Plane::Transform()` — origin, xaxis, yaxis and zaxis all transformed consistently — and the result is handed to `ReplaceFacePlaneConvexPlanar()`, which does the actual re-trim of every face. A pure translation vector alone would NOT have been a genuine generalization of `OffsetFace()`: a plane's geometry is invariant under moving its own origin WITHIN the plane, so only a translation's component along the face's own normal is ever observable — exactly what `OffsetFace()`'s own `distance` already expresses. This function is a real generalization only because `xform` can also ROTATE the face's own frame, which neither `OffsetFace()` nor a plain translation vector can do at all, and unlike `FoldFaceConvexPlanar()`/`DraftFacesConvexPlanar()`, the rotation isn't tied to a hinge edge or a caller-supplied neutral plane — any axis and center work. Verified two ways: (1) fed `ON_Xform::TranslationTransformation(distance * old_plane.zaxis)`, it reproduces `OffsetFace()`'s own result bit-for-bit, vertex for vertex (`TestMoveFaceConvexPlanarMatchesOffsetFaceForPureNormalTranslate`, tests/test_basic.cpp) — proof the translation path is a genuine generalization, not a separate and possibly-divergent construction; (2) a real rotation about an axis through the face's own current plane origin (making that origin the rotation's fixed point) leaves that exact point on the new plane and rotates the normal away from the original by precisely the given angle (`cos(angle) == new_normal . old_normal` to 1e-9) — an algebraic rigid-body fact independent of this function's own half-space-clip arithmetic, and something no translation vector could ever produce (`TestMoveFaceConvexPlanarRotationMatchesExactAngleAndFixedOrigin`). Refusal cases (out-of-range `face_index`, a singular/non-invertible `xform` collapsing the face's own frame to an invalid plane) are also covered (`TestMoveFaceConvexPlanarRefusesInvalidInput`). - [present] Re-intersect adjacent faces / rebuild edges after an edit (post-tweak edge regeneration) — **upgraded from partial: the "only tested on planar surfaces" gap is closed this pass (app wiring remains, but doesn't block present — see below).** App `RebuildEdgesReal` (cmd_fillet.cpp:2527) refits every 2-trim edge through the real surface-surface intersection of its faces. `ReplaceEdgeCurve` (see that bullet's own detail elsewhere in this category) re-trims faces against WHATEVER substitute curve a caller hands it — it never computed one from the two faces' own actual geometry itself, the exact "no automatic kernel-level re-intersection after a tweak" gap this bullet used to describe. `Brep::RebuildEdgeCurve(edge_index, tolerance)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/brep.h; dino8-kernel/src/brep.cpp) now exists: it runs the kernel's own general SSX intersector (`IntersectSurfaces()`, dino8/kernel/surface_intersect.h — the same Newton-polished mesh-seeded surface/surface intersector `ImprintFaces()`/`SplitFaceByCurve()` already build on, general to ANY `ON_Surface` pair, not enumerated per surface-type, and NOT restricted to convex planar solids the way most of this category's other siblings are) between `edge_index`'s own two bordering faces' real, UNTRIMMED surfaces, then locates the sub-arc that actually lands on this edge by finding each candidate curve's own closest parameter to the edge's existing two vertices (`CurveClosestParamGlobal`) and requiring both matches land within `tolerance` — a pair of faces can genuinely meet along more than one component (e.g. two cylinders crossing twice), so every candidate is checked, not just the first. Deliberately the UNTRIMMED intersector, not the trim-aware `IntersectFaces()`: a real shared edge runs exactly ALONG the trim boundary of both its own bordering faces the entire way (that is what "these two faces meet along this edge" means), and `IntersectFaces()`'s own inside/outside trim classification — built for a curve that CROSSES a boundary, e.g. `ImprintFaces()`'s piercing case — degenerately treats every sample sitting exactly ON that boundary as outside and clips the whole curve away to nothing (confirmed directly: on two hand-built perpendicular faces sharing a genuine edge, `IntersectFaces()` returned zero curves while `IntersectSurfaces()` on the identical two surfaces found exactly the expected line; caught by this session's own first attempt at this function, which used `IntersectFaces()` and failed its own tests before the switch). The matched sub-arc (not the raw curve's own full extent, which may run past the trimmed edge on either side) is resampled and refit via `InterpolateCubic()` and handed to `ReplaceEdgeCurve()` to commit — "compute the true intersection, extract the matching span, delegate the re-trim." `Brep::RebuildAllEdgeCurves(tolerance)` is the one-call "rebuild every qualifying edge in this Brep" sibling, the same single/all pairing `RemoveHoleLoop()`/`RemoveAllHoleLoopsInBrep()` already give theirs; since `ReplaceEdgeCurve()` never calls `Compact()`, one pass over every live edge (no rescan needed) suffices, and it counts only edges whose curve GENUINELY changed (sampled and compared to the pre-rebuild curve), not mere attempts. Verified on two hand-built perpendicular planar faces (the z=0 and y=0 planes, each surface's own full domain extending well past the shared boundary in the other, non-shared direction): perturbing the shared edge's own curve into a same-endpoints bulge sagging off the true x-axis line, then calling `RebuildEdgeCurve`, recovers the two planes' own EXACT analytic intersection (every sampled point's y and z components under 1e-6, not merely closer than before) with the same two endpoints preserved (`TestBrepRebuildEdgeCurveRecoversExactPlaneIntersectionAfterPerturbation`, tests/test_basic.cpp); `RebuildAllEdgeCurves` on the same re-perturbed fixture rebuilds exactly the one qualifying (2-trim) edge and reports 0 on a second pass once nothing is left to change. Also verified to refuse rather than invent a curve: a naked (1-trim) edge (out of this method's own two-face scope), and two PARALLEL planes forced to share a fabricated edge — the two surfaces genuinely never cross anywhere — both return `Result::Failed` leaving the Brep untouched, alongside the usual out-of-range/already-deleted `edge_index` throws (`TestBrepRebuildEdgeCurveRefusesInvalidInput`). - [partial] Push/pull a face (extrude face and merge/cut into its own body) — **corrected: upgraded from missing.** Kernel `PushPullFace(solid, face_index, distance)` (boolean.h/boolean.cpp) landed this session: a push (`distance > 0`) genuinely extrudes new side-wall faces into previously-empty space without touching any other face (unlike `OffsetFace`, which always re-extends/re-trims neighbours in place); a pull (`distance < 0`) retrims every neighbour via an exact single half-space clip and adds no new geometry. Direct topological surgery, not a boolean — `Brep::Extrude()`+`BooleanCombinePlanar()` was tried first and found to fail (a swept profile is only piecewise planar; even a hand-built all-planar prism makes `BooleanCombinePlanar()` throw on the flush, zero-overlap coincident face this operation always creates, a disclosed gap in that engine's own coincident-face handling). No convexity precondition on `solid` (verified on a genuinely non-convex L-shaped prism, both directions). **2026-10-05: the "a pull refuses an oblique (non-perpendicular) neighbour" restriction this bullet used to name is closed.** `SplitByHalfspace()` (the half-space clip a pull's own retrim already runs, `dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/detail/halfspace_clip3d.h`) was always a genuine 3D-plane clip, exact for ANY neighbour plane regardless of orientation — the actual bug was in `new_loop` itself, which used to translate every one of the pulled face's own boundary vertices uniformly along its normal, correct only when every incident neighbour is perpendicular to that normal (the neighbour's own plane then contains the normal direction, so sliding a shared vertex along it stays exactly in that plane) and silently WRONG for an oblique neighbour (the translated vertex leaves that neighbour's own plane entirely, leaving a gap between the new cap and the neighbour's own correctly-clipped boundary). The fix, `PushPullCorrectedVertex()` (`dino8-kernel/src/boolean.cpp`, new private helper used by both `PushPullFace` and `PushPullFaces`): at a Brep vertex where the pulled face meets two neighbours, a THIRD edge — shared between those two neighbours themselves, not with the pulled face — runs from that vertex into the solid's own interior; clipping either neighbour against the same cut plane finds its own crossing point on that identical physical 3D edge, so both neighbours necessarily agree on the corrected vertex position no matter which plane either one lies on. `new_loop`'s own corner there is now computed directly as that edge's real intersection with the cut plane (found via `FindSharedEdgeIndices()`, the same opposite-winding shared-edge match `FacesShareEdge()` already uses, extended to also report WHERE the match is in each loop) instead of a blind per-vertex offset — for a perpendicular neighbour this reduces algebraically to the exact same point the old offset already gave, so every pre-existing test in this family is unaffected (confirmed: all pass unchanged). Verified on a genuine frustum (`DraftFacesConvexPlanar` tilting all 4 walls of a 10x10x10 box about its own base — the identical construction `TestDraftFacesConvexPlanarBoxAllWallsMatchesExactFrustumVolume` already builds and verifies independently), whose 4 side walls are confirmed NOT perpendicular to the top cap's own normal (`std::fabs(zaxis.z) > 0.05` checked directly, not assumed): pulling the top face down by 4 (new height 6) matches the classical frustum-of-a-pyramid volume formula `(h/3)(A0+A1+sqrt(A0*A1))` at the NEW height exactly (530.88, to 1e-9 relative) — not the volume a blindly-translated top cap would give — and the new top cap itself lands on the EXACT concentric `[0.6,9.4]x[0.6,9.4]` square the frustum's own linear taper implies, not the old `[1,9]x[1,9]` square merely moved down by 4 a naive offset would have produced (`TestPushPullFaceObliqueNeighbourMatchesExactFrustumVolume`, tests/test_basic.cpp); the result still tessellates to a closed, watertight manifold, and a large enough pull that collapses an oblique wall's own retrimmed boundary to nothing is still correctly refused (`std::invalid_argument`), now via the same "fewer than 3 vertices" check reached for an oblique case for the first time rather than the old blanket perpendicularity gate. `PushPullFaces()`'s own identical restriction is lifted the same way, verified to match `PushPullFace()`'s own output bit-for-bit vertex-for-vertex on the same frustum (`TestPushPullFacesObliqueNeighbourMatchesPushPullFace`). Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite rebuilt and run clean: 9238 checks, 0 failures, 0 regressions (up from 9170, the current branch-head baseline after the merged curve-operations/data-exchange rounds). Still partial: planar-faced solids only (`PlanarFaces()`'s own precondition, unchanged), and no `dino8-app` command wiring exists for `PushPullFace`/`PushPullFaces` yet.

  *Same-day follow-up (this pass): this pass adds a genuine batch sibling, still partial.* `PushPullFaces(solid, face_distances)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/boolean.h; dino8-kernel/src/boolean.cpp) now exists: `face_distances` is a caller-chosen list of `(face_index, distance)` pairs - the same two positional arguments `PushPullFace()` takes for one face at a time - applied in a single call. This is genuinely load-bearing, not merely fewer function calls for the same result: a PULL retrims every perpendicular neighbour it touches, so calling `PushPullFace()` twice in sequence runs the SECOND call against whatever intermediate boundary the FIRST call already left its neighbours at - order-dependent in a way a single combined call never is, since this function derives every named face's own new cap and every unnamed neighbour's own clip from `solid`'s own ORIGINAL geometry exactly once. Two named faces that share an edge are refused outright (each would independently want to redraw the OTHER's own shared boundary - a pushed face's new side wall starts at its old edge, a pulled neighbour's own retrim ends at a new, closer one - genuinely ambiguous, not attempted), the same "no silent tie-break" discipline `MoveFacesConvexPlanar()`/`ReplaceFacePlanesConvexPlanar()` already enforce for a duplicate target, applied here to adjacency instead of identity. Verified two ways: (1) a single-entry `face_distances` list reproduces `PushPullFace()`'s own output bit-for-bit, vertex for vertex, in both the push and pull direction (`TestPushPullFacesSingleEntryMatchesPushPullFace`, tests/test_basic.cpp) — proof the batch's shared reconstruction introduces no divergence of its own; (2) pushing the box's own front wall out while independently pulling its (non-adjacent, opposite) back wall in, in ONE call, matches the exact volume arithmetic and — matched face-for-face by centroid and vertex-count rather than by raw PlanarFaces() index order, since `PushPullFace()`'s own new-face append position depends on which face was named and so genuinely differs between the two sequential orders and the batch — the identical solid two SEQUENTIAL single `PushPullFace()` calls produce in EITHER order (front-then-back or back-then-front), proving the batch's own one-pass consistency doesn't merely happen to match one arbitrary calling order (`TestPushPullFacesTwoIndependentPushPullMatchesEitherSequentialOrder`). Refusal cases — an empty `face_distances`, an out-of-range `face_index`, a zero/non-finite distance, a duplicate `face_index`, and two adjacent named targets (the box's own front and top walls) — are also covered (`TestPushPullFacesRefusesInvalidInput`). - [partial] Analytic/analytic SSX closed forms (plane/plane, plane/cylinder, cylinder/cylinder, plane/sphere, cone, torus) — closed forms still exist only inside `BooleanCombineMixed`'s private splitters (`SplitCylindricalByObliquePlane`, `SplitCylindricalByParallelCylinder`, Steinmetz/unequal-cylinder splitters) and the planar boolean's plane/plane path. No public analytic-SSX API, and no plane/sphere, cone or torus closed form (the only general path is the mesh-seeded `IntersectSurfaces`).

  *2026-10-05, a seventh kernel rotation on this category (round 15): closes the "plane/sphere" half of this bullet's own named list with a genuine public closed form.* `IntersectPlaneSphere(plane, sphere, tolerance)` (dino8-kernel/include/dino8/kernel/surface_intersect.h; src/surface_intersect.cpp) solves the true geometric relation directly — the sphere center's signed distance `d` from the plane (`ON_Plane::DistanceTo`), the resulting circle's own center at the center's projection onto the plane, radius `sqrt(r^2 - d^2)` — with no mesh seeding and no Newton polish at all, honestly degenerating to a single tangent point when `|d|` is within `tolerance` of `r` and to a genuine miss (`empty == true`) when `|d| > r + tolerance`. Converted to its own NURBS form via `ON_Circle::GetNurbForm`, the same exact-conversion primitive `Brep::Sphere()`/`Cone()`/`Torus()` already rely on elsewhere in this kernel. Verified by `TestIntersectPlaneSphereClosedForm` (tests/test_basic.cpp): a sphere centered exactly on the plane produces the hand-derivable full-radius great circle (every sampled point of the fitted curve confirmed on-plane and at exactly the sphere's own radius); a sphere resting tangent to the plane from above reports a tangent point at the hand-derivable origin; a sphere held well clear of the plane reports a genuine miss; a sphere crossing the plane off-center produces a circle of the hand-derivable `sqrt(r^2 - d^2)` radius, centered at the correct projected point; and a zero-radius sphere is refused outright rather than treated as a degenerate circle. Still honestly scoped: only this one analytic pair is closed — plane/cylinder, cylinder/cylinder, plane/cone, and plane/torus remain exactly as unaddressed as before, still existing only inside `BooleanCombineMixed`'s own private splitters, not as a public API; this also does not replace `IntersectSurfaces()` for a plane/sphere pair arriving as two generic `ON_Surface` references with no sphere-ness known to the caller. Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite (direct run): 8897 checks, 0 failures, 0 regressions.

  *2026-10-05, round 17 on this category: closes the "plane/cylinder" half and narrows the "cylinder/cylinder" half of this same named list, both genuine closed forms, no mesh seeding, no Newton polish.* `IntersectPlaneCylinder(plane, cylinder, tolerance)` (surface_intersect.h/.cpp) solves the plane/cylinder case directly: for a plane edge-on to the cylinder's own axis (axis lies IN the plane, to within an internal angular tolerance), the axis's own signed distance to the plane is constant along its whole length, so `cos(phi) = -d/radius` gives the 0/1/2 genuine line crossings (each parallel to the axis) with no iteration at all; otherwise the result is a true ellipse — a true circle in the special case the axis is exactly perpendicular to the plane, the SAME formula handling both without a separate branch — built from its own exact orthogonal semi-axis pair (minor = `radius`, along `cross(plane.zaxis, axis)`; major = `radius * sqrt(1 + (B/C)^2)` for the `B`/`C` the function derives from the plane/axis geometry directly) rather than the non-orthogonal `(e0, e1)` basis the private `ComputeEllipseFrame3d` (ellipse_clip3d.h) uses internally for its own, different purpose (clipping a polygon against the ellipse boundary, not reporting the ellipse's own true semi-axes) — so this is a fresh, independent derivation suited to a public API, not a re-export of that private helper. Deliberately scoped to the cylinder's INFINITE lateral surface along its own axis (an `ON_Cylinder` built with a finite `height` is not trimmed to that range here), the same unbounded scope `IntersectPlaneSphere()` already takes for a sphere. Verified by `TestIntersectPlaneCylinderClosedForm` (tests/test_basic.cpp): a perpendicular cut reports a true circle (`ON_Ellipse::IsCircle()`) at the hand-derivable center and radius; a 60-degree oblique cut through the axis reports a real ellipse whose semi-minor is the exact cylinder radius and whose semi-major matches the hand-derivable `radius / cos(60deg) = 2*radius`, every sampled curve point confirmed to lie on both the cutting plane and the cylinder's own lateral surface simultaneously; an edge-on plane through the axis reports the hand-derivable two-ruling crossing, one exactly tangent reports the single-line degeneracy, and one held clear reports a genuine miss; a zero-radius cylinder is refused outright. `IntersectCylinderCylinderParallel(a, b, tolerance)` (surface_intersect.h/.cpp) is a public extraction of the SAME closed form `BooleanCombineMixed`'s own private `ComputeParallelCylinderCrossing` (boolean.cpp) already uses for its own angular-split bookkeeping (standard circle/circle intersection — Weisstein/MathWorld; Bourke, 1997 — of the two cylinders' cross-sectional circles, projected into any plane perpendicular to their shared axis direction), but returning the actual 3D line(s) a caller needs rather than that private helper's own angle-only bookkeeping, and refusing outright (`not_parallel`) rather than silently misanswering when the two axes genuinely are not parallel — the general, non-parallel-axis cylinder/cylinder pair remains exactly as unaddressed as before. Verified by `TestIntersectCylinderCylinderParallelClosedForm` (tests/test_basic.cpp): two genuinely crossing cylinders report two lines, each independently confirmed to sit at exactly both cylinders' own radii from their respective axes simultaneously (not via a hardcoded decimal expectation); externally tangent cylinders report the single-line degeneracy at the hand-derivable tangent point; disjoint and fully-nested pairs both report a genuine miss; concentric (same-axis) cylinders report the disclosed non-result (no well-defined 2D lens exists there) rather than a fabricated line; non-parallel axes are refused outright; and a zero-radius operand is refused. Neither addition flips this bullet's own count-affecting status (`[partial]` stays `[partial]` — cylinder/cylinder's own general, non-parallel case and the plane/cone, plane/torus pairs remain unaddressed), the same "narrows without flipping" shape this category's own earlier rounds already established for a still-partial item; no `dino8-app` command calls either new function yet. Full `dino8_kernel_tests` suite (direct run, after both additions and both tests): 9136 checks, 0 failures, 0 regressions (9104 immediately before this round's own 32 new checks: 20 from `TestIntersectPlaneCylinderClosedForm`, 12 from `TestIntersectCylinderCylinderParallelClosedForm`).

  *2026-10-06, round 18 on this category: closes the "plane/plane" half of this same named list - the easiest of its remaining pairs, and, like the others, previously a public-API gap even though the planar boolean's own plane/plane path already had an internal closed form.* `IntersectPlanePlane(a, b, tolerance)` (surface_intersect.h/.cpp) solves the classical relation directly: writing each plane's own unit normal/offset as `n, h = dot(n, origin)`, a point common to both planes decomposes as `alpha*n_a + beta*n_b` (the only directions that can move either dot product) via the 2x2 system `alpha + beta*c == h_a`, `alpha*c + beta == h_b` (`c = dot(n_a, n_b)`), solved directly - no mesh seeding, no Newton polish, the same style `IntersectPlaneSphere`/`IntersectPlaneCylinder` already established for this bullet's other pairs. When the two normals are parallel (`c`'s own cross product with the other normal is near zero, the formula's own denominator degenerating), this checks `b`'s own distance to `a`'s plane directly instead: within tolerance means the SAME plane (`coincident == true`, no single line exists), otherwise two genuinely parallel, disjoint planes (a genuine miss). Verified by `TestIntersectPlanePlaneClosedForm` (tests/test_basic.cpp): a hand-derivable axis-aligned crossing (the horizontal z=0 plane against the vertical x=0 plane, meeting exactly along the y-axis) confirmed at two different points along the reported line; a general oblique pair verified not against a hardcoded expected line but against the defining property itself (every sampled point of the reported line lies on BOTH original planes' own implicit equations simultaneously, at `t = 0, 1, -3.7`); two different descriptions of the literal same plane report the coincident degeneracy; two genuinely parallel, distinct planes report a genuine miss; and an invalid (zero-normal) plane is refused outright.
